new_entities.name: Chronic metoclopramide use
new_entities.description: Repeated or prolonged metoclopramide exposure beyond short-course antiemetic use.

new_entities.name: Tardive dyskinesia
new_entities.description: Often persistent involuntary movements, especially of the face, mouth, or tongue, associated with chronic dopamine-blocking drug exposure.

edges.effect_quant: In a matched VA prevalence study, metoclopramide users had a relative risk of 1.67 for tardive dyskinesia versus controls, while a 2019 review estimated absolute risk around 0.1% per 1000 patient-years but concentrated in elderly, diabetic, and other neurologically vulnerable groups.
edges.population: adults receiving repeated or long-term metoclopramide, especially older adults, diabetics, and patients with other neurologic susceptibility factors
edges.mechanism: Chronic dopamine D2 receptor blockade in basal ganglia circuits can trigger maladaptive receptor and signaling changes that eventually manifest as persistent involuntary movements even after the drug is stopped.
edges.summary: Chronic metoclopramide exposure clearly carries a tardive dyskinesia risk, although modern reviews suggest the absolute rate is lower than older regulatory estimates implied. The harm remains clinically important because the syndrome can be prolonged or irreversible in a subset of patients.
edges.caveats: Absolute risk estimates vary by population, ascertainment method, and exposure duration. Risk is not uniform: elderly women, diabetics, people with renal or hepatic impairment, and those on concomitant dopamine-blocking drugs appear to be at much higher risk than healthier short-course users.
